events.title: The Guardian reveals bulk collection of Verizon call records, then PRISM
events.summary: On 5 June 2013 The Guardian published a top-secret Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court order, granted on 25 April, requiring Verizon to hand the NSA call records 'on an ongoing, daily basis', including domestic calls. A second story reported an NSA programme called PRISM, described in a 41-slide training presentation, that collected search history, email content, file transfers and live chats from Google, Facebook, Apple and other US internet companies; the companies denied knowledge of it. The US Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board later dated the first story to 5 June 2013 and described it as the first of a series based on documents disclosed by Edward Snowden.
events.significance: Showed that privacy's walls had moved inside the phone network and the cloud, where people could neither see nor object to collection — the grievance that later drove Schrems, the GDPR's enforcement and demands for user-side controls.

sources.title: NSA collecting phone records of millions of Verizon customers daily
sources.quote: The order, a copy of which has been obtained by the Guardian, requires Verizon on an "ongoing, daily basis" to give the NSA information on all telephone calls in its systems , both within the US and between the US and other countries.
sources.note: The page now shows a timestamp of Thu 6 June 2013 06.05 EDT (a later update); the story first appeared on the evening of 5 June US time. The space before the comma is in the page text.

sources.institution: Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board (US)
sources.title: Report on the Telephone Records Program Conducted under Section 215 of the USA PATRIOT Act and on the Operations of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court
sources.quote: On June 5, 2013, the British newspaper The Guardian published the first of a series of articles based on unauthorized disclosures of classified documents by Edward Snowden, a contractor for the National Security Agency (“NSA”).

sources.title: NSA Prism program taps in to user data of Apple, Google and others
sources.quote: The NSA access is part of a previously undisclosed program called Prism , which allows officials to collect material including search history, the content of emails, file transfers and live chats, the document says.
sources.note: URL dated 6 June 2013; the page timestamp (7 June 2013 15.23 EDT) reflects a later update.

events.locationNote: The Guardian's London headquarters at Kings Place; the Verizon story was reported by Glenn Greenwald from Hong Kong and edited in London and New York.

events.title: Edward Snowden identifies himself as the source, from Hong Kong
events.summary: On 9 June 2013 The Guardian named its source, at his request, as Edward Snowden, a 29-year-old former CIA technical assistant then employed by the contractor Booz Allen Hamilton, who had worked at the NSA for four years through outside contractors. He had flown to Hong Kong on 20 May.
events.significance: Put a human face on the gap between what people had agreed to and what was being done with their data, making surveillance a mass public issue across the democracies.

sources.title: Edward Snowden: the whistleblower behind the NSA surveillance revelations
sources.quote: Edward Snowden , a 29-year-old former technical assistant for the CIA and current employee of the defence contractor Booz Allen Hamilton. Snowden has been working at the National Security Agency for the last four years as an employee of various outside contractors, including Booz Allen and Dell.
sources.note: The space before the comma is in the page text. Same article: 'The Guardian, after several days of interviews, is revealing his identity at his request.' and 'On May 20, he boarded a flight to Hong Kong, where he has remained ever since.'

sources.title: Edward Snowden: the whistleblower behind the NSA surveillance revelations
sources.quote: On May 20, he boarded a flight to Hong Kong, where he has remained ever since.

events.locationNote: City-level coordinates (Tsim Sha Tsui, Kowloon), where Snowden met the journalists; the exact hotel is not cited here.

events.title: EU Court of Justice: search engines must delist on request (Google Spain)
events.place: Court of Justice of the European Union, Kirchberg, Luxembourg
events.summary: In Case C-131/12, brought after Mario Costeja González complained in 2010 to Spain's data protection agency about search results linking to 1998 La Vanguardia pages announcing a real-estate auction, the Grand Chamber held that a search engine operator processes personal data and can be obliged to remove links to lawful third-party pages from results for a person's name. It held that the data subject's rights under Articles 7 and 8 of the Charter override, as a rule, both the operator's economic interest and the public's interest in finding the information, unless the person's role in public life justifies access.
events.significance: Established that an individual can make a claim directly against a global platform about how information on them is surfaced — a person-initiated request with legal force, the first widely used 'right to be forgotten'.

sources.institution: Court of Justice of the European Union (Grand Chamber), via EU Publications Office (Cellar)
sources.title: Judgment of the Court (Grand Chamber) of 13 May 2014, Google Spain SL and Google Inc. v Agencia Española de Protección de Datos (AEPD) and Mario Costeja González, Case C-131/12, EU:C:2014:317
sources.quote: As the data subject may, in the light of his fundamental rights under Articles 7 and 8 of the Charter, request that the information in question no longer be made available to the general public by its inclusion in such a list of results, it should be held, as follows in particular from paragraph 81 of the present judgment, that those rights override, as a rule, not only the economic interest of the operator of the search engine but also the interest of the general public in finding that information upon a search relating to the data subject’s name.
sources.note: Paragraph 97. curia.europa.eu's judgment viewer blocks scripted access; the identical official text is served by the EU Publications Office repository (CELEX 62012CJ0131).

sources.institution: Court of Justice of the European Union
sources.title: Press Release No 70/14: Judgment in Case C-131/12 Google Spain SL, Google Inc. v Agencia Española de Protección de Datos, Mario Costeja González
sources.quote: In 2010 Mario Costeja González, a Spanish national, lodged with the Agencia Española de Protección de Datos (Spanish Data Protection Agency, the AEPD) a complaint against La Vanguardia Ediciones SL (the publisher of a daily newspaper with a large circulation in Spain, in particular in Catalonia) and against Google Spain and Google Inc.

events.locationNote: Seat of the Court of Justice, Luxembourg.

events.title: Schrems I: the EU Court of Justice strikes down Safe Harbour
events.place: Court of Justice of the European Union, Kirchberg, Luxembourg
events.summary: Maximillian Schrems, an Austrian Facebook user since 2008, complained to the Irish Data Protection Commissioner that, in light of Snowden's 2013 revelations, US law did not protect data transferred there from surveillance. In Case C-362/14 the Grand Chamber declared the Commission's 2000 Safe Harbour decision (2000/520) invalid, holding that laws allowing public authorities generalised access to the content of electronic communications compromise the essence of the right to private life.
events.significance: One individual's complaint dismantled the legal basis for transatlantic data flows, proving that a person could force the system to answer for where their data goes.

sources.institution: Court of Justice of the European Union (Grand Chamber), via EU Publications Office (Cellar)
sources.title: Judgment of the Court (Grand Chamber) of 6 October 2015, Maximillian Schrems v Data Protection Commissioner, Case C-362/14, EU:C:2015:650
sources.quote: In particular, legislation permitting the public authorities to have access on a generalised basis to the content of electronic communications must be regarded as compromising the essence of the fundamental right to respect for private life, as guaranteed by Article 7 of the Charter
sources.note: Paragraph 94. Operative part: 'Decision 2000/520 is invalid.' Official text via the EU Publications Office repository (CELEX 62014CJ0362).

sources.institution: Court of Justice of the European Union
sources.title: Press Release No 117/15: The Court of Justice declares that the Commission's US Safe Harbour Decision is invalid
sources.quote: Maximillian Schrems, an Austrian citizen, has been a Facebook user since 2008.

events.locationNote: Seat of the Court of Justice, Luxembourg.

events.title: The European Commission adopts the EU-US Privacy Shield
events.summary: Nine months after Safe Harbour fell, the Commission adopted Implementing Decision (EU) 2016/1250, finding that the United States ensured an adequate level of protection for personal data transferred to organisations that self-certified under a new EU-US Privacy Shield. The Court of Justice invalidated this decision four years later in Schrems II.
events.significance: A replacement negotiated between governments, not with the people whose data moved — and it did not survive judicial review.

sources.institution: European Commission (Official Journal of the European Union L 207, 1.8.2016), via EU Publications Office (Cellar)
sources.title: Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2016/1250 of 12 July 2016 on the adequacy of the protection provided by the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield
sources.quote: Based on the findings developed in recitals 136-140, the Commission concludes that the United States ensures an adequate level of protection for personal data transferred under the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield from the Union to self-certified organisations in the United States.
sources.note: Recital 141; signed 'Done at Brussels, 12 July 2016.' Official text via the EU Publications Office repository (CELEX 32016D1250).

events.title: Schrems II: the Court of Justice invalidates Privacy Shield
events.place: Court of Justice of the European Union, Kirchberg, Luxembourg
events.summary: On a reference from the Irish High Court in Case C-311/18, the Grand Chamber declared Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2016/1250 on the EU-US Privacy Shield invalid, while holding that the Commission's standard contractual clauses (Decision 2010/87) remained valid. It was Schrems's second successful challenge to the legal basis of EU-US data transfers.
events.significance: Confirmed that under the GDPR the individual's rights travel with the data, and that no political deal can override them without real redress.

sources.institution: Court of Justice of the European Union (Grand Chamber), via EU Publications Office (Cellar)
sources.title: Judgment of the Court (Grand Chamber) of 16 July 2020, Data Protection Commissioner v Facebook Ireland Ltd and Maximillian Schrems, Case C-311/18, EU:C:2020:559
sources.quote: Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2016/1250 of 12 July 2016 pursuant to Directive 95/46/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council on the adequacy of the protection provided by the EU-US Privacy Shield is invalid.
sources.note: Operative part, point 5. Official text via the EU Publications Office repository (CELEX 62018CJ0311).

sources.institution: Court of Justice of the European Union
sources.title: Press Release No 91/20: The Court of Justice invalidates Decision 2016/1250 on the adequacy of the protection provided by the EU-US Data Protection Shield
sources.quote: However, it considers that Commission Decision 2010/87 on standard contractual clauses for the transfer of personal data to processors established in third countries is valid.

events.locationNote: Seat of the Court of Justice, Luxembourg (judgment delivered during COVID-19 restrictions).

events.title: Third attempt: the EU-US Data Privacy Framework
events.summary: After Schrems II, the United States adopted Executive Order 14086 on 7 October 2022, limiting signals-intelligence collection and creating a Data Protection Review Court. On 10 July 2023 the Commission adopted Implementing Decision (EU) 2023/1795, finding that the United States ensures an adequate level of protection for data transferred to organisations certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework.
events.significance: The third transatlantic arrangement in eight years, it shows how contested the legal plumbing under every data flow remains — and why terms that travel with the person, not the pipe, are attractive.

sources.institution: European Commission (Official Journal of the European Union L 231, 20.9.2023), via EU Publications Office (Cellar)
sources.title: Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2023/1795 of 10 July 2023 on the adequate level of protection of personal data under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework
sources.quote: As a result of these discussions, the United States on 7 October 2022 adopted Executive Order 14086 ‘Enhancing Safeguards for US Signals Intelligence Activities’ (EO 14086), which is complemented by a Regulation on the Data Protection Review Court issued by the U.S. Attorney General (AG Regulation)
sources.note: Recital 6; signed 'Done at Brussels, 10 July 2023.' Official text via the EU Publications Office repository (CELEX 32023D1795).

sources.institution: European Commission (Official Journal of the European Union L 231, 20.9.2023), via EU Publications Office (Cellar)
sources.title: Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2023/1795 of 10 July 2023 — adequacy finding
sources.quote: Based on the findings set out in recitals 9-200, the Commission concludes that the United States ensures an adequate level of protection for personal data transferred under the EU-U.S. DPF from a controller or a processor in the Union
